listenings.text: Right, let me take you through this quickly and then you can ask me whatever you want. What the numbers show is inflammation, and it has been there for a while, which is not the same as saying it is new. What they do not show, and I want to be clear about this, is anything that has deteriorated since your last screening two years ago. Nothing has got worse. Now, what I would like you to do. Walk before breakfast rather than in the evening, because you will actually do it, and the routine matters far more than the intensity. Twenty minutes every day beats an hour twice a week, every time. And two things before you go. Do not stop taking the tablets without telling me first, whatever you read online. And remember to book the next screening at the desk before you leave the building, because if you leave it until you are home you will not do it.

There are two answers to how are you and most people only own one of them. The first is fine, thank you. It is true, it is polite, and it ends the subject in four words. The second is the whole file. Fourteen minutes of dates and tablets and a scan from 2019, at a table where four people were about to talk about something else, and now nobody can leave. The middle setting takes about eight seconds and it has a shape. One fact. One measure of what it costs you. And then a question that hands the conversation back to somebody else. It is chronic rather than serious, so I am managing it rather than fixing it, and it takes a toll on me, although less than it did last year. What about you, are you still running? Now, in a consulting room, everything I have just said reverses. There you should be boring. Give the date it started. Say what has changed and what has not. Say what you stopped taking and in which month. And never, ever round a number downwards to make it sound better, which is exactly what people do when they are frightened.

extra_audio.text: Ruth says that after forty years as a physician the question she was worst at answering was how are you. She explains that the short answer is still the right one socially, and that the skill is the sentence after it. She gives the shape of the middle register: one fact, one measure of the cost, and the conversation handed back. Braulio admits that he stopped taking one of his tablets in March and has never said so out loud in English. Ruth tells him that in a consulting room the rule reverses, and that nobody should ever round a number to sound better.

reading.rtitle: The Register Between Fine and Fourteen Minutes
paras: There are two answers to the question how are you, and most people only own one of them. The first is fine, thank you, which is true, polite and finished. The second is the whole file: fourteen minutes of dates, tablets and a scan from 2019, delivered at a table where four other people were about to talk about something else.

The middle setting has a shape, and it takes about eight seconds. One fact, one measure of what it costs you, and then a question that hands the conversation back. It is chronic rather than serious, so I am managing it rather than fixing it. It takes a toll on me, although less than it did last year. What about you, are you still running? Nobody is trapped, nothing has been hidden, and the subject moves on because you moved it.

In a consulting room, in a country where you do not speak the language, that rule reverses completely. There you should be boring. Give the date it started. Say what has deteriorated and what has not. Say what you stopped taking and in which month. Say whether the last screening found anything. And never round a number downwards to make it sound better, which is precisely what most people do when they are frightened, and which costs a doctor the one thing he cannot get anywhere else.

Underneath both registers sits one small grammatical trap that changes a sentence into its own opposite. I stopped smoking means you are not a smoker. I stopped to smoke means you interrupted your walk to have a cigarette. I remember reading it is a memory; remember to read it is an instruction. The form ending in -ing points backwards at something real, and the form with to points forwards at something intended. Behind you, or ahead of you.
reading.source: Article -- The Long View, a newsletter about work and what comes after it
